title: Psalm 129: Plowed Over, but Not Overcome
summary: Israel is called to declare that it has been attacked over and over since its youth, its back plowed like a field, yet its enemies have never prevailed, because the righteous LORD cut the cords of the wicked. The psalm then prays that those who hate Zion will wither like grass on a rooftop, useless for any harvest, with no one passing by to bless them.
story: Psalm 128 closed with a blessing on a household and on Israel. Psalm 129 remembers why Israel's survival is not to be taken for granted. The same call to the congregation that opened Psalm 124 (“let Israel now declare”) returns here, and the psalm reviews a whole national history of suffering in a few lines. It moves from the family table of Psalm 128 to the scarred back of a nation, and it prepares for the cry from the depths in Psalm 130. In the Songs of Ascents, pilgrims going up to Zion remembered not only God's blessings but the long hostility the people and the city had survived.
historical:
The heading names no author, only “A song of ascents”. The psalm is a review of Israel's history from its youth, a phrase the prophets used for Israel's beginnings in Egypt and the wilderness (Hosea 2:15; 11:1; Jeremiah 2:2). From there the history included oppression in Egypt, wars with Canaanite peoples and Philistines, the Assyrian conquest of the northern kingdom in 722 BC, the Babylonian destruction of Jerusalem in 587 or 586 BC, and the exile. Many scholars date the psalm after the exile, when that long history lay behind the community and when it faced hostile neighbors; others think it could come from the monarchy. The psalm names no specific enemies, which allows it to cover the whole story.

The prayer in verses 5-8 is against “all who hate Zion”, meaning those who oppose God's chosen city and the worship centered there. The psalm does not pray for the defeat of foreigners as such, but for the failure of hostility against God's purposes in Zion.
cultural:
Plowing in ancient Israel was done with a simple wooden plow, sometimes tipped with iron, pulled by oxen and guided by a farmer who cut long, straight furrows through the soil. The picture of plowmen plowing over Israel's back is shocking. It may describe a people lying face-down while enemies walk over them (Isaiah 51:23 uses a similar image), or the deep wounds left by whipping. The cords of verse 4 continue the farm picture: they are the ropes that bind the plow to the oxen, so to cut them is to stop the plowing.

Houses in Israel had flat roofs made of beams covered with packed earth. Seeds blew onto them and sprouted after rain, but with no depth of soil the grass withered quickly in the sun, useless to anyone (2 Kings 19:26 uses the same picture for nations overrun by Assyria). Harvest workers greeted each other with blessings; in the book of Ruth, Boaz greets his reapers in the name of the LORD and they answer with a blessing (Ruth 2:4). Verse 8 imagines a field so barren that no such greeting will ever be spoken over it.
literary: Psalm 129 has two parts. Verses 1-4 are a communal statement of trust, opening with a call to the congregation and a stair-step repetition: “Many a time they have persecuted me from my youth” appears in verses 1 and 2, with the second line adding the turn, “but they have not prevailed against me.” Verses 5-8 are a prayer against the enemies, built on agricultural images that echo the first half: Israel's back was plowed, but its enemies will be like grass that never reaches the harvest. The psalm speaks of the nation as “me”, a single person who has survived. The final line is ironic: the blessing of the LORD, normally spoken at harvest, is withheld because there is no harvest to bless.

outline.t: The plowed back and the cut cords
May Zion's haters wither like rooftop grass

doctrines.note: Israel has survived not because it was strong but because the LORD is righteous and cut the cords that bound it. The psalm reads a long history of suffering as also a history of preservation.

The prayer that Zion's enemies will wither is a request that God's justice prevail over those who oppose his purposes. It leaves the judgment in God's hands rather than calling for Israel to take revenge.
The psalm does not deny how much Israel has suffered. It names the persecution plainly, many times over, and holds it together with the confession that the persecutors did not prevail.

words.note: Tsarar, to bind, press, or harass. It describes pressure and hostility, the action of an enemy who hems someone in. Repeated in verses 1 and 2, it sums up Israel's long experience of oppression, from Egypt onward.

Charash, to plow, and also to devise or plot. The word appears twice in verse 3 in its plowing sense, but its other meaning adds an echo: those who plowed over Israel's back also plotted against it. The image of furrows cut long into a back is one of the most vivid pictures of suffering in the Psalms.

Avot, cord or rope. It is the harness that ties oxen to a plow or binds a prisoner. When the LORD cuts the cords of the wicked, the plowing stops; the image shows deliverance as God breaking the apparatus of oppression.

christ: The New Testament does not quote Psalm 129, but Christian readers have long heard in its third verse an image of the suffering of Christ. The servant in Isaiah 50:6 says he gave his back to those who struck him, and the Gospels record that Jesus was flogged before his crucifixion (Matthew 27:26; John 19:1). He took on himself the suffering Israel describes, and the same pattern held in him that the psalm confesses of Israel: the enemies did not prevail, because God raised him. Jesus also promised that the gates of Hades would not overcome his church (Matthew 16:18), a promise with the same shape as verse 2. The connection is typological, a pattern in Israel's history fulfilled in Christ, not a prediction within the psalm itself.

hard.q: How should Christians read the prayer that God's enemies wither and receive no blessing?
hard.a: Psalm 129's second half belongs to a group of psalms, sometimes called imprecatory psalms, that ask God to bring disaster on enemies, and they trouble many readers because Jesus taught his followers to love their enemies and bless those who curse them (Luke 6:27-28). Some interpreters see these prayers as a stage of revelation that the gospel moves beyond. Others note that they hand vengeance over to God rather than taking it, which is what Paul also asks of believers (Romans 12:19), and that they express a real longing for justice against those who oppose God. Psalm 129's prayer is also comparatively restrained: it asks that hatred of Zion come to nothing, not for bloodshed. Many readers pray it today as a prayer against the powers that oppose God's purposes, while praying for the people caught up in them.

questions: Israel remembers its sufferings in one breath with its survival. When you look back on hard seasons, what do you remember first: the plowing, or the cords being cut?
What do you think it meant for pilgrims to recite a history of suffering on the way up to worship?
How do you pray about people or powers that oppose what is good? What does this psalm add to that prayer, and what does Jesus add?
